name: When to trade pieces
goal: You can decide when to trade: when you are ahead in material, to remove a strong enemy piece, or to escape an attack, and when to keep pieces on.

intro.text: Every trade changes the position, so before you make one, ask what it does for you. When you are ahead in material, trades make your extra material count, because your opponent has fewer pieces left to fight back with. Trade off your opponent's best piece, and the piece that is attacking your king. But when you are the one attacking, or you are behind, keep the pieces on the board.

parts.title: Ahead? Trade queens
parts.keyIdea: When you are ahead in material, trade pieces, above all the queens: fewer pieces left means fewer chances for your opponent.
parts.text: From a game played on Lichess. You are White and three pawns up. Black's queen has just come to f3, the only black piece close to your king.

credit.authors: Lichess; the players of the game

notes.text: Offer the queen trade. Your bishop on d3 guards e2, so if Black takes, you take back. Without queens your king is safe, and three extra pawns will count for a lot in the endgame.
Take back. Two bishops and three extra pawns against a knight and a bishop is a winning endgame, and your king is now free to walk up the board and help the pawns.

parts.title: Remove their best piece
parts.keyIdea: A piece that dominates the board is worth trading off, even for a piece of the same value.
parts.text: From a game played on Lichess. You are Black, and White's knight has just jumped to e6, deep in your half of the board.

credit.authors: Lichess; the players of the game

notes.text: The knight on e6 is White's best piece: the pawn on d5 guards it, none of your pawns can ever chase it away, and it attacks your rook on f8. Trade it off with your bishop.
Not 27...Qxe6 at once: 28.exf5 would hit your queen with a pawn, and that is what happened in the game. Push the f-pawn past White's e-pawn first, and take on e6 next move.
Now take the pawn. You are two pawns up, and your knight on e5 can never be chased away by a white pawn, because White has no d-pawn or f-pawn left.

parts.title: Trade off the attacker
parts.keyIdea: If one enemy piece is doing all the attacking near your king, offer to trade it off.
parts.text: From a game played on Lichess. You are White and ahead in material, but Black's queen on h3 has come right up to your king.

credit.authors: Lichess; the players of the game

notes.text: Black's queen is the only black piece near your king. Offer the trade on g4, where your pawn on f3 guards your queen. Whether the queens come off or Black's queen goes back, the danger to your king is over.
Take back with the pawn. With the queens off, your king is safe and your extra material counts for more.
Now use your extra rook: put it on the open d-file, ready to go to d7 on Black's second rank.

parts.title: Keep the queens when you attack
parts.keyIdea: When the enemy king is out in the open, avoid trading queens: your queen is your best attacker.
parts.text: From a game played on Lichess. You are White. Black's queen on b5 attacks yours and offers a trade, but Black's king is standing out in the open on e6.

credit.authors: Lichess; the players of the game

notes.text: Do not trade. After 36.Qxb5 axb5 the endgame would be about equal, but with the queens on, Black's king on e6 is in danger. Move your queen away with check.
Keep adding pressure: the h-pawn attacks g6 to open more lines towards Black's king.
